How to read this report

Scores assess the local pages’ intent, usefulness, distinctiveness, evidence and crawlable structure. They are editorial judgments, not Google scores or measured traffic performance. Utility pages are unscored. The separate public homepage assessment is 5/10.

P0: public availability for the portfolio. P1: first content improvements. P2: subsequent work. P3: lower acquisition priority. The first commercial shortlist is based on content fit, not validated keyword demand.

Ahrefs returned “Insufficient plan”; Semrush returned “no_api_units.” Rankings, traffic, search volumes, Google indexing and measured Core Web Vitals remain unverified. No production page or application source was changed.

Full findings and recommendations

Cubusify organic search audit — 20 October 2026

The biggest constraint is deployment: the public domain serves a different one-page website. Of the 84 routes in the current portfolio source, 83 return HTTP 404 on https://cubusify.com/. Improving those local pages alone will not make them available to search engines.

Scope and interpretation

  • Rendered every current source route on the server and inspected its main content, headings, metadata definitions, images and links. This avoids relying on the older build, which contains 85 routes and some content that differs from the current source.
  • Made unauthenticated HTTP GET requests to all 84 canonical route URLs. Results: homepage 200, remaining 83 routes 404. The public homepage differs from the local homepage.
  • Checked public robots.txt and sitemap.xml: both return 200. Robots allows crawling. The sitemap lists only the homepage.
  • Both www.cubusify.com and cubusify.com return 200 for the homepage; both declare the non-www canonical. Prefer a permanent redirect to the chosen hostname to make this consistent.
  • Ahrefs project discovery failed with Insufficient plan. Semrush discovery returned no_api_units. No Search Console clicks, impressions, rankings, search volumes, backlink metrics or analytics were retrieved.
  • No browser rendering, measured Core Web Vitals, or form delivery test was performed. HTTP accessibility does not prove Google indexing.

Scores are editorial SEO-readiness judgments out of 10, not measured traffic performance or a Google/vendor score. They consider intent clarity, content usefulness, distinctiveness, evidence/trust and crawlable structure. A reusable layout is fine; repeated answers with little new service information are the issue. There is no target word count. Utility pages are not scored as traffic opportunities. Local readiness scores do not override the live 404 status.

Read all page ratings in CSV, all page ratings in Markdown, or raw audit evidence. A copy of the publicly fetched homepage is in live-homepage.html. JSON includes text, headings, links and response details for each page.

For the 33 non-AI specialist pages, the nearest specialist-page match shares 86.9–91.8% of unique five-word phrases, measured with Jaccard similarity on main text after excluding scripts, styles and SVG. This includes shared process/gallery language and is a diagnostic comparison, not a Google penalty score. The source confirms that these pages use the same parent content object and substitute the hero title and introduction. Some sibling-card lists also link back to the page itself.

Examples: Shopify and WooCommerce development need separate information about theme work, checkout constraints, migrations, integrations and handover. “MVP development” needs discovery outputs, scope decisions, milestones and evidence of relevant work. A new heading alone is insufficient.

Potential overlaps to resolve through clearer scope and, later, Search Console evidence:

  • /services/software/saas-platforms and /services/product/saas-engineering
  • /services/marketing/search-engine-optimisation and /services/seo-aeo-geo
  • /services/ecommerce and /industries/ecommerce

Overlap is a risk, not verified keyword cannibalisation. Do not redirect or canonicalise distinct services blindly. Retain separate pages when they answer different buyer needs; consolidate only after defining intent and examining available query/link data.

Public homepage: 5/10 editorial readiness

The live page has a descriptive title and H1, canonical URL, readable HTML, service summaries, process, FAQs and an enquiry route. These are useful foundations.

However, its service links are section anchors rather than distinct service landing pages. It offers little detailed evidence for individual services. Its HTML still contains testimonial instructions such as “Add a real quote from a happy client here” and placeholder client names. Remove these placeholders or replace them with approved, genuine testimonials; do not publish invented replacements. Browser visibility was not tested, but this material is present in the returned page HTML.

The one-page sitemap itself is appropriate for the current one-page website. The issue is that the intended portfolio and its service/article pages are absent from the public domain.

Technical foundations worth keeping

The current source renders one H1 on each route, uses image alt attributes, and has no unresolved main-content internal page links in the route inventory. The prerendering pipeline generates HTML, canonical URLs, robots directives, sitemap entries and applicable structured data. The older build also contains unique titles and descriptions across its 85 pages. These are useful foundations, but the older saved audit is not evidence of the current public deployment.

53 current metadata descriptions are shorter than 80 characters, often because they are one-line service blurbs. This is not a length violation; improve descriptions where they fail to explain the actual offer and reason to visit. Titles such as “Custom CRM” and “Healthcare” need clearer intent more than arbitrary character padding.

Search-oriented heading examples that preserve room for the existing brand voice:

  • Homepage: “Custom Software Development & AI Automation”
  • /services/ecommerce/shopify-development: “Shopify Development Services”
  • /services/software/custom-crm: “Custom CRM Development Services”
  • /services/product/mvp-development: “MVP Development for Startups” if this is the intended customer
  • /industries/healthcare: “Healthcare Software Development”

These are editorial suggestions, not keywords validated for volume, difficulty or geography.

Order of work for organic growth

  1. Resolve public availability. Confirm that cubusify.com is the intended production destination, then deploy the approved portfolio when authorised. Check each chosen route returns 200 with its own content and canonical; check sitemap coverage, public access and a real 404 response for nonexistent pages. Do not treat adding a sitemap as a substitute for deploying pages. No deployment was performed in this audit.
  2. Establish a search baseline. Verify the domain in Google Search Console, submit the production sitemap and inspect representative URLs. Record page/query clicks, impressions, CTR and average position, plus country/device and date ranges. Track qualified enquiries separately from traffic. A site search result is not a complete index inventory.
  3. Focus the first commercial rewrites. Start with AI/business automation, custom CRM, Shopify development and MVP development if these reflect the services the business most wants to sell. Give each a defined buyer, problem, deliverables, implementation choices, integrations, unique FAQs and a genuine example. This shortlist is based on existing content fit and commercial specificity, not measured demand. Confirm target countries, customer types and real service priorities before commissioning extensive content.
  4. Connect the strongest existing articles to those offers. Keep the useful article structures, clarify titles and attribution, add original examples, and use descriptive contextual links. Article → relevant specialist service → genuine example → enquiry is the intended journey. The weak service destinations need improvement alongside the articles.
  5. Build verifiable proof. Add actual project narratives with permission: problem, constraints, contribution, decisions and observed outcomes. Keep concept demonstrations clearly labelled. Substantiate homepage counters/recognition and keep company identity consistent across the website and genuine business profiles.
  6. Expand only around demonstrated gaps. Use queries, sales questions and relevant search results to decide the next pages. Do not create more generic service pages or bulk city pages. If local business demand matters, validate the actual location and service area before developing a local search plan.

Suggested work sequence: availability and measurement first; two focused service rewrites next; connect the three strongest articles; then expand the next two services using what the first batch reveals. Once data exists, prioritise relevant pages already getting impressions around positions 5–20, then pages with weak CTR relative to comparable queries. Compare similar date ranges and record changes; search impact can take longer than a work cycle.

Measurement and remaining unknowns

Success means more relevant organic visits and qualified enquiries, not just a higher audit score. Track non-brand clicks to service pages, article-to-service visits, organic enquiry conversion and lead fit. Add measurement consistent with the site's actual tracking/consent setup.

Unknown: current Google indexing, search demand by market, actual rankings, inbound authority, real-user performance and the approved production deployment destination. No numerical traffic uplift or ranking forecast is supportable from the available evidence.

Guidance used

  • Google: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content — descriptive headings, original value, clear attribution and evidence of expertise; no preferred word count.
  • Google: JavaScript SEO basics — crawlable links, rendered content and meaningful HTTP responses.

No application source, production setting or deployed page was changed. The saved deliverables are audit files only.

      Home/Insights/SEARCH & GROWTHSEARCH & GROWTHSEO, AEO and GEO: where should your business start?A practical plan for clearer search visibility, useful answers and a website people can trust.By Cubusify Editorial · Updated 18 October 2026On this pageWhat do SEO, AEO and GEO mean?Choose one customer journey to improveUse structured data accuratelyAgree what success looks likeWhat to considerStart with your highest-priority service and the questions buyers ask before contacting you.Keep technical search foundations, content and conversion improvements in one plan.Measure qualified enquiries as well as visibility.A growing business usually has a practical question: what should we improve first to bring more suitable enquiries? Start with a service page that explains who you help, what you deliver and how a project begins. Search visibility is only useful when a visitor can understand the offer and take the next step.What do SEO, AEO and GEO mean?FocusWhat it meansUseful workSEOSearch engine optimizationCrawlable pages, clear structure and useful content.AEOAnswer engine optimizationClear responses to specific customer questions.GEOGenerative engine optimizationUseful, attributable information for AI-assisted discovery.Google’s current guidance treats optimization for its generative AI search features as part of SEO. The fundamentals still matter: useful original content, accessible pages and a clear technical structure. Eligibility does not guarantee indexing or inclusion. Read Google’s guide to generative AI search.Choose one customer journey to improveFor example, a manufacturer seeking a production dashboard needs to understand the problems it can solve, which systems it connects to, how implementation is scoped and what information to prepare. A page that answers those questions gives the buyer a more useful starting point than a long list of technologies.Choose a priority service and define the type of enquiry you want.List the questions your sales team hears repeatedly.Review the current page on a phone: can a buyer find the answer and contact you?Add relevant examples, a clear process and a practical next step.Check that page titles, links and navigation describe the actual content.Use structured data accuratelyStructured data describes page content in a machine-readable format. Use applicable types and keep the markup consistent with what visitors can see. It does not guarantee a rich result or AI citation. See Google’s structured data introduction.Agree what success looks likeRecord a baseline for the priority page before changing it.Track relevant search queries, landing-page visits and completed enquiries.Review enquiry quality: service fit, budget, location and readiness.Compare a meaningful period and account for seasonality before drawing conclusions.At Cubusify, we bring the technical review, page improvements and measurement plan together.       Home/Insights/ECOMMERCEECOMMERCEShopify, WooCommerce or a custom store?Start with your catalogue, operations and growth plans.By Cubusify Editorial · Updated 18 October 2026On this pageWhat is the real difference between Shopify, WooCommerce and a custom store?How large and complex is your catalogue?Who will run the store every day?What about integrations, ERP and checkout customisation?What does total cost of ownership include?How do performance, hosting and SEO control compare?Shopify vs WooCommerce vs custom: side-by-side comparisonWhen does headless or custom make sense, and what is the migration risk?What to do nextWhat to considerShopify is hosted and managed for you, WooCommerce is a WordPress plugin you host yourself, and a custom store is software built around your own rules.The deciding factors are usually who runs the store day to day, how complex your catalogue is, and which systems must connect to it, not the feature list.Compare total cost of ownership, not the build quote: hosting, apps or plugins, maintenance, payment fees and developer time all recur.Choose custom or headless only when a specific, revenue-relevant journey cannot be done on a standard platform.Replatforming carries real SEO and data risk, so plan URL redirects, product data migration and a rollback path before you commit.Shopify vs WooCommerce comes down to who runs the store and how unusual your way of selling is. Shopify is a hosted platform that looks after the infrastructure for you. WooCommerce is a plugin for WordPress that you host and maintain yourself. A custom store is worth building only when a standard platform cannot support a journey that earns you money.The best choice is rarely the platform with the longest feature list. It is the one your team can run on an ordinary Tuesday without calling a developer, and that will still fit the business in two years. This guide gives you the criteria, a comparison table and a short process for deciding.What is the real difference between Shopify, WooCommerce and a custom store?The real difference is who carries responsibility. With Shopify, a vendor hosts the platform, runs the checkout infrastructure and ships core updates, and you configure the store, choose a theme and add apps. With WooCommerce, you or your agency choose hosting, update WordPress, the plugin and every extension, and take care of security and backups. With a custom store, you own all of it.That gives you a simple way to think about it. Shopify trades some flexibility for convenience. WooCommerce trades convenience for control over the code, the database and the content. Custom trades speed and low upkeep for the freedom to model your business exactly. None of the three is better in general. Each is better for a particular kind of team.How large and complex is your catalogue?Catalogue complexity matters more than catalogue size. A few thousand simple products with sizes and colours suit all three options. Trouble starts with unusual structures: made-to-order products with many dependent options, bundles with rules, B2B price lists per customer, rental or booking items, or products that need a configurator before they can be priced.Ask three questions. Can every product be described as a title, images, variants and a price? Do prices or availability depend on who is buying? Does a buyer need to configure the product before adding it to the basket? If the answers are yes, no and no, a hosted platform is usually the quickest route. If the second or third answer is yes, list exactly which rules you need and check whether a maintained app or plugin covers them before you consider custom work.Who will run the store every day?The person who edits products, processes orders and runs promotions should shape the decision. A marketing or operations lead who wants to launch a collection or a discount without developer help usually does well on Shopify, because the admin is built for merchants. A team that already publishes content on WordPress may find WooCommerce natural, because products, posts and landing pages live in one system.Custom admin tools can be excellent when they are designed around your exact workflow, but they only help if someone owns their evolution. Be honest about capacity. If nobody on the team can look after plugin updates, backups and hosting, a self-hosted store will slowly become a risk. If you want deep control and have a developer or agency on retainer, that same setup becomes an asset.Rule of thumbChoose the platform your least technical daily user can operate confidently. A powerful system that only one developer understands is a business risk, not an advantage.What about integrations, ERP and checkout customisation?Integrations decide more projects than design does. Write down every system the store must exchange data with: inventory or ERP, accounting, shipping, a CRM, a marketing tool, a returns process. For each one, note what moves in which direction and how often. Stock levels and orders are the usual pain points, because errors there cost money and customer trust.Shopify extends through apps and APIs, and its documentation describes checkout customisation through checkout UI extensions and Shopify Functions, which let you add interface elements and change business logic such as discounts, delivery options and payment rules. WooCommerce is extended with PHP hooks, filters, plugins and its REST API, so almost anything is possible but quality varies by plugin. A custom store lets you design the integration properly, at the price of building and maintaining it.If you run an ERP, ask early whether a maintained connector exists for your platform and who supports it when it breaks. Our integration solutions work often starts exactly here, with a clear data map between the store and the systems behind it.Related interface showcase. Illustrates product capabilities; it is not evidence of a client result.What does total cost of ownership include?Total cost of ownership is everything you pay to build, run and change the store over its life, not the build quote. Prices and plans change often, so check each vendor’s current pricing page rather than relying on an article. What you should do is list the cost categories so the three options are compared like for like.Platform or hosting: a subscription for a hosted platform, or hosting, a CDN and backups for a self-hosted one.Theme and design work, including future changes to templates.Apps or plugins, which often carry their own recurring fees, and the effort of keeping them compatible.Payment provider and transaction fees, which depend on your provider, region and plan.Developer time for integrations, bug fixes, updates and security patching.Staff time: how many hours a week your team spends working around limitations.Migration and exit costs if you outgrow the choice.Custom builds have the highest upfront cost and often the lowest per-feature friction later, but they also have the largest maintenance obligation. Hosted platforms look cheaper at the start and can accumulate app fees. Self-hosted WooCommerce can look cheapest on paper and then quietly cost developer hours. Model three years, not three months.How do performance, hosting and SEO control compare?Hosting responsibility is the clearest performance difference. On Shopify the platform handles servers and delivery, so your speed depends mostly on your theme, images and apps. On WooCommerce, speed also depends on your host, caching, database and plugin load, which gives you more control and more ways to go wrong. On a custom store, performance is whatever you engineer.For search, all three can rank well when built properly. WooCommerce sits on WordPress and offers fine control over URLs, templates and content. Shopify gives you editable titles, descriptions, redirects and sitemaps, though some URL patterns such as the products and collections prefixes are fixed. Custom stores give full control but require you to build SEO basics deliberately. Whichever route you take, plan for performance and search foundations, clean product data and structured markup from the start.Shopify vs WooCommerce vs custom: side-by-side comparisonUse this table to score each option against your own priorities. It describes general tendencies, not guarantees, so confirm the details for your own requirements before you decide. Give each row a weight from one to three based on how much it matters to your business, then see which column wins.Shopify, WooCommerce and custom ecommerce compared across the main decision criteriaCriterionShopifyWooCommerceCustom storeHosting modelHosted and managed by the vendorSelf-hosted on WordPress; you choose and manage hostingYou choose and manage everythingBest for catalogueStandard products and variantsContent-rich or moderately unusual cataloguesComplex configurators, rules and pricingDay-to-day adminMerchant-friendly, built for non-developersFamiliar if you already use WordPress; more upkeepWhatever is built; needs an ownerCheckout customisationThrough extensions and Shopify FunctionsHooks, filters and plugins; wide but uneven qualityFully designed to your rulesIntegrations and ERPApps and APIs; check connector supportPlugins and REST API; check maintenanceBuilt to your exact data flowsCost shape over timeSubscription plus apps and feesHosting, plugins and developer timeHighest upfront, ongoing engineeringPerformance responsibilityPlatform infrastructure; you manage theme and appsShared: host, caching, pluginsEntirely yoursSEO controlGood, with some fixed URL patternsVery high with WordPress toolingTotal, but built from scratchMigration risk laterModerate; data export and redirects neededModerate; you own the data and databaseHigher; custom data models are harder to moveWhen does headless or custom make sense, and what is the migration risk?Custom or headless commerce makes sense when a specific journey earns real revenue and a standard platform cannot support it. Headless means the shopping interface is built separately from the commerce engine and talks to it through an API. It can give you a faster, fully tailored front end, but it also means you maintain two layers, and many conveniences of a themed store become your responsibility.Good reasons include a product configurator, unusual B2B pricing, a subscription model with special rules, or an experience that spans content, community and commerce. Weak reasons include wanting a unique look alone, or assuming custom is automatically faster. Our custom ecommerce team tends to suggest proving the hardest journey with a small prototype first.Replatforming itself is risky whichever way you go. Products, customers, order history, reviews and URLs all have to move, and any URL that changes without a redirect can lose search visibility. Keep the old store running until the new one is verified, redirect every important URL, and agree a rollback path. Our search and visibility service includes a review of redirects, indexing and monitoring needs.Related interface showcase. Illustrates product capabilities; it is not evidence of a client result.What to do nextTake an hour and do three things. List your ten most important products and any rules attached to them. List every system the store must connect to. Name the person who will run the store daily. With those three lists, most teams can already rule out one option.Then test the hardest journey, not the easiest. If you are leaning towards a hosted platform, our Shopify development work focuses on theme, catalogue and checkout. If WordPress is already part of your stack, see WooCommerce development. If neither fits, bring your list to a conversation and we will help you judge it honestly. You can contact us whenever you are ready.Discuss your projectFor clearer search foundations and useful answers, explore our SEO, AEO and GEO services.CONTINUE READINGAnother useful perspective.SEO, AEO and GEO: where should your business start? ↗Where AI automation is actually useful. ↗Plan a smaller, stronger first MVP. ↗

      Home/Insights/AI & AUTOMATIONAI & AUTOMATIONWhere AI automation is actually useful.Look for repeatable work before choosing a model.By Cubusify Editorial · Updated 18 October 2026On this pageWhat makes a task worth automating with AI?Which seven workflows should you automate first?How do you rank the seven for your business?What should you not automate yet?How do you run a first pilot?What to do nextWhat to considerAI automation for business works best on tasks that repeat often, have a clear owner and can be checked quickly by a person.Start with workflows where a mistake is cheap to catch, such as drafting replies for approval, before touching anything that moves money or sends messages on its own.Every workflow needs a number you can measure before and after, such as minutes per task, first response time or share of drafts accepted without edits.Rank candidates by frequency, cost of error, data availability and ease, then pilot one workflow on real examples before building more.Some work should not be automated yet: unclear processes, high-stakes decisions and anything with no sample data to test against.AI automation for business means using AI models inside a defined workflow so that software handles the routine reading, sorting and drafting, while people handle the decisions. It is most useful on tasks that repeat often, follow a recognisable pattern and can be checked quickly.It is least useful when sold as a replacement for judgement. This guide gives seven workflows that usually make good first projects, a table to rank them for your own business, and a list of work that should wait. Each workflow is described the same way: what goes in, what the AI does, what a person still checks, and how to measure it.What makes a task worth automating with AI?A task is worth automating when it repeats often, has a clear owner, produces an output someone can check in seconds, and has examples you can test against. If you cannot describe the input, the expected output and what counts as a mistake, the task is not ready for AI yet.Four questions help. How often does it happen? What does a wrong result cost? Do you have past examples to test with? How many other systems must it connect to? A weekly task with expensive errors and no examples is a poor first project. A daily task with cheap errors and a shared inbox full of examples is a good one. Write down the current time per task before you start, because that is your baseline for every claim later.Which seven workflows should you automate first?These seven appear in most small and mid-sized businesses in some form. They are listed roughly from lowest risk to highest. In every case the AI prepares and a person approves, at least until you have evidence that the output is reliable enough to relax that rule.1. Enquiry triage and routingGoes in: emails, web form messages or chat enquiries.AI does: labels the type (sales, support, billing, spam), extracts key details such as company, product and urgency, and routes it to the right queue.Person checks: low-confidence items and a regular sample of routed ones.Measure: time from arrival to the right person seeing it, and the share of enquiries rerouted by hand.This is often the best first project because mistakes are visible and cheap to fix. A misrouted enquiry is slower, not catastrophic. Our business automation service typically starts here.2. Drafting replies for human approvalGoes in: a customer message plus your policies, past replies and product information.AI does: writes a draft reply in your tone and cites which policy or past answer it used.Person checks: every draft before it is sent, editing as needed.Measure: drafts accepted with no or light edits, minutes saved per reply, and complaints about tone or accuracy.Nothing is sent without approval, so the risk stays low while you learn how often the drafts are good. Edits are also useful data: patterns in what people change show you where the instructions or source documents need work.3. Document and invoice data extractionGoes in: invoices, purchase orders, forms, contracts or delivery notes, often as PDFs or photos.AI does: pulls out named fields such as supplier, date, line items and totals into a structured record.Person checks: fields that fail validation, such as totals that do not add up, and a sample of the rest.Measure: field-level accuracy against a hand-checked set, and time per document.Accuracy here can be measured field by field, which makes it one of the more honest workflows to evaluate. Add simple rules around the AI, for example rejecting a record where line items do not sum to the total.4. Meeting and call note summaries into the CRMGoes in: a call recording transcript or meeting notes, with permission from participants.AI does: summarises decisions, lists action items with owners, and proposes updates to CRM fields.Person checks: the summary and any CRM change before it is saved.Measure: minutes spent on admin after calls, and how many CRM records are complete a day later.The value is mostly consistency: notes get written and records get updated. Make sure you have consent to record and transcribe, and decide where transcripts are stored and for how long. A custom CRM can make the proposed updates easier to review.5. Internal knowledge searchGoes in: handbooks, policies, product sheets, past proposals and help articles.AI does: answers staff questions in plain language and shows the source passages it used.Person checks: the cited source when the answer matters, and owners review gaps the assistant reports.Measure: questions answered without asking a colleague, share of answers with a correct source, and searches that end in no result.This is the workflow behind most AI assistants. It only works as well as your documents, so budget time to clean them. Explore how a business AI assistant can use your own information with appropriate access controls.Related interface showcase. Illustrates product capabilities; it is not evidence of a client result.6. Lead qualification and follow-up prepGoes in: new leads from forms, ads or events, plus your definition of a good fit.AI does: summarises the company from public information, scores fit against your criteria, and drafts a first follow-up for the salesperson.Person checks: the score and the draft before anyone is contacted.Measure: time from lead to first contact, and whether high-scored leads convert better than low-scored ones.Track the last measure honestly. If scores do not predict outcomes, change the criteria rather than trust the number. See our sales and marketing automation work for how routing and follow-up preparation fit together.7. Report and dashboard commentaryGoes in: figures from your reports or business dashboards, plus last period for comparison.AI does: drafts a short written commentary on what changed and which numbers look unusual.Person checks: every figure quoted and every explanation offered, since the AI sees the numbers but not the reasons.Measure: time to produce the weekly report, and corrections made before it is shared.Keep the calculations in code or your reporting tool, not in the model. Let the AI describe numbers that are already computed, then have an analyst confirm the explanations.How do you rank the seven for your business?Score each candidate on four things: how often it happens, how costly a mistake is, whether you have example data, and how easy it is to connect. The table below shows a typical starting view. Treat the ratings as a prompt for discussion, because your business will differ.Typical starting ratings. Adjust to your own volumes and risks.WorkflowFrequencyCost of errorData availabilityEaseEnquiry triage and routingHighLowHigh (inbox history)MediumDraft replies for approvalHighLow (approved first)High (sent mail)MediumDocument and invoice extractionMedium to highMediumMediumMediumMeeting and call notes to CRMMediumLow to mediumMediumMediumInternal knowledge searchMediumLow to mediumDepends on document qualityMediumLead qualification and follow-up prepMediumMediumMediumMedium to hardReport and dashboard commentaryLow to medium (weekly)MediumHigh (the numbers exist)Easy to mediumPick the row where frequency is high, error cost is low and data exists. For many teams that is enquiry triage or drafted replies. If your biggest pain is somewhere else, such as invoices, start there, but add stricter validation because the cost of an error is higher.Rule of thumbIf you would be uncomfortable with a new hire doing the task on day one without review, the AI should not do it without review either. Begin with review, then relax it where your measurements justify it.What should you not automate yet?Leave a task alone when the process is unclear, a wrong answer is costly or irreversible, or you have no examples to test against. Automating a messy process produces a faster mess. These tasks are better left with people, or automated only up to a drafting step.Processes nobody can describe. Write the steps down first. If two people do it differently, agree one way before adding AI.Final decisions on money, contracts, hiring, health or legal matters. AI can prepare material, but a named person decides.Anything that sends messages or changes records with no review, until you have measured error rates on real examples.Tasks with no sample data. Without 30 to 50 real, representative cases you cannot tell whether the workflow works.Sensitive personal or confidential data you have not classified. Decide what may leave your systems before choosing tools.Rare, high-variety work such as one-off negotiations, where each case is different and the saving is small.How do you run a first pilot?Run one workflow, on real examples, with a person approving the output, and compare it with your baseline. A small pilot answers whether the workflow works for your data far more cheaply than a large build, and it shows where the real work is: usually in documents, permissions and integrations, not the model.Choose one workflow and write down its current time per task and error rate.Collect 30 to 50 real examples, including awkward ones, and agree what a good output looks like.Build the smallest version that connects to the real inbox, CRM or document store, with approval before anything is sent or saved.Run it alongside the current process for a set period and log accepted, edited and rejected outputs.Review the numbers, fix the biggest failure pattern, then decide whether to widen, change or stop.Related interface showcase. Illustrates product capabilities; it is not evidence of a client result.Plan for the unglamorous parts too: logging, access rights, a clear handoff when the AI is unsure, and someone who owns the workflow after launch. Demos show the idea; production needs these. If you are unsure whether you need a simple assistant, a workflow or something more autonomous, explore our AI and automation services first.What to do nextPick the workflow with the highest frequency, lowest cost of error and best example data, and measure how long it takes today. That one number is the start of a useful conversation about scope. You do not need a model chosen or a vendor shortlisted to do this.If you would like help ranking your own candidates or scoping a pilot, tell us which task is eating the most time through our contact page. We work in milestones with regular demos and agree what success looks like before building. Cost and timing depend on scope, so we talk them through with you rather than quote a number here.Discuss your projectFor clearer search foundations and useful answers, explore our SEO, AEO and GEO services.CONTINUE READINGAnother useful perspective.SEO, AEO and GEO: where should your business start? ↗Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom store? ↗Plan a smaller, stronger first MVP. ↗

      Home/Insights/PRODUCT ENGINEERINGPRODUCT ENGINEERINGPlan a smaller, stronger first MVP.Build the journey that tests your most important assumption.By Cubusify Editorial · Updated 18 October 2026On this pageWhat is a minimum viable product, and what is it not?How do you choose one customer, one problem and one journey?Which assumption should you test first?How do you scope MVP features with must, should and could?Should you build, buy or use no-code for the first test?How do you set milestones and success metrics before building?How can AI help plan an MVP without replacing user conversations?When is an MVP the wrong tool?What to do nextWhat to considerAn MVP is a learning tool: it exists to test your riskiest assumption with real users, not to ship a cheaper copy of the whole product.Scope around one customer, one problem and one complete journey that a user can start, finish and understand.Sort every feature into must, should or could, and cut anything you could do by hand for your first ten users.Define milestones as working outcomes and agree success metrics before building, so the result is a decision rather than an opinion.AI can speed up prototyping and research, but it cannot replace conversations with real customers.MVP development is the practice of building the smallest working version of a product that can test your riskiest assumption with real users. A minimum viable product is not a rough demo and not a thinned-out copy of your full vision. It is a complete but narrow first version: one customer, one problem and one journey that works from start to finish.To plan an MVP, name the customer and the problem, list your assumptions and pick the riskiest, sort features into must, should and could, and cut hard. Then define milestones as working outcomes and agree your success metrics before anyone writes code. The sections below take each step in turn, including when an MVP is the wrong tool.What is a minimum viable product, and what is it not?A minimum viable product is the smallest version of a product that delivers real value to a real user and teaches you something you could not learn by thinking. The word "minimum" limits the scope. The word "viable" sets the bar: someone must be able to complete a task and get a result they care about. Unlike a prototype, which may only show an idea, an MVP has to work for a user, even if it is narrow, manual in places and plain to look at.The most common mistake is treating the MVP as version one of the full product, with every feature made thinner. That gives you a wide, shallow build that tests nothing. A better frame is a question. For example, "will clinic managers stop using a paper diary if booking takes two taps?" is a question an MVP can answer. "Will people like our platform?" is not.How do you choose one customer, one problem and one journey?Choose the customer who feels the problem most often and already works around it, whether with a spreadsheet, a stack of messages or a paid tool they dislike. Narrow beats broad. A product for "small businesses" cannot be tested, because their needs differ too much. A product for one type of team with one painful weekly task can be. The workaround you can see today is evidence that the problem is real.Then write the journey as one sentence: "A customer can complete one task and see the result without help." If the sentence needs three "and" clauses, it is really three journeys. Pick the one that, if it worked, would make the customer say they would switch or pay. Everything else waits.Who exactly is the first user, and how will you reach ten of them?What do they do today instead, and what does it cost them in time or errors?What is the single action that proves they got value?What must be true before they can start, such as data, access or an account?One-sentence ruleIf you cannot describe the journey in one sentence, or you cannot name ten real people who could try it, the scope is still too wide or the customer too vague. Fix that before you plan any features.Related interface showcase. Illustrates product capabilities; it is not evidence of a client result.Which assumption should you test first?Test the assumption that would end the project if it were wrong and for which you have the least evidence. Every product rests on assumptions about whether people want it (desirability), whether you can build it (feasibility) and whether the business works (viability). Assumption mapping makes them visible, so your first weeks go to the one that matters most rather than the one that is easiest to build.List every assumption behind your idea, one per line, such as "managers will enter the data themselves" or "customers will pay monthly".Score each one for the damage if it is wrong and for how little evidence you have today.Circle the ones that score high on both. These are your riskiest assumptions.Pick one and design the smallest test that could prove it wrong.Decide in advance what result would make you continue, change direction or stop.Often the riskiest assumption is not technical. It is "will they change their habit?" or "will they give us access to their data?" Test those with a conversation or a clickable mock-up first, and save engineering for assumptions only working software can test.How do you scope MVP features with must, should and could?Sort every candidate feature by one test: does the core journey fail without it? If yes, it is a must. If the journey works but is clumsier, it is a should. If it is merely nice to have, it is a could. Be strict: a real MVP scope has a short list of musts and a long list of coulds you will not touch.A scoping table for a hypothetical appointment-booking MVPBucketTest to applyExample featuresDecisionMustThe journey fails without itChoose a time slot, confirm the booking, see the confirmationBuild nowShouldThe journey works but is clumsier without itEmail reminder, reschedule linkBuild only if time remains after the mustsCouldNice to have, and no user has asked for it yetCalendar sync, loyalty points, custom themesLeave out and note in a backlogNot nowA real need, but risky or costly for a first testOnline payments, multiple locations, role permissionsReplace with a manual step or deferCutting is where most MVPs are won or lost. Common things to remove from a first version include admin panels (use a database view or spreadsheet instead), user roles and permissions (start with one role), settings pages, multiple payment methods, polished onboarding, reporting suites and integrations with tools your first users do not rely on. Each can be replaced by a manual step.Do it by hand firstIf a person can do a task for your first ten customers, do it by hand and learn from doing it. Automate it only once you know it matters and you understand how it really works.Should you build, buy or use no-code for the first test?Use the cheapest tool that can still answer your question. For a first test that may be a configured SaaS product, a no-code builder or a form connected to a spreadsheet. Custom code makes sense when the journey itself is the product, when a no-code tool cannot deliver the experience users need, or when the demand is already proven and you want to build it properly.Choosing a route for the first testRouteBest whenWatch out forBuild customThe experience or logic is the product, or you need control over data and performanceHighest upfront effort, and it is easy to build more than the test needsBuy or configure SaaSA standard tool already covers most of the journeyPer-user costs and limits on how far you can change itNo-code or low-codeYou need a working interface quickly to test demandLimits on scale, performance and data portability; a rebuild may followConcierge or manualYou are unsure the customer wants the outcome at allDoes not scale and does not test technical feasibilityNone of these choices is permanent. Many good products began as a no-code test and were rebuilt once demand was proven. If you are weighing longer-term tooling rather than a quick test, our custom software team can help assess the criteria.Related interface showcase. Illustrates product capabilities; it is not evidence of a client result.Can you fake the product first? The concierge and Wizard of Oz shortcutYes, and it is often the fastest route to learning. In a concierge MVP you deliver the outcome by hand and the customer knows it: you are the product. In a Wizard of Oz MVP the customer sees a working interface while people do the work behind it. Both test whether the outcome is wanted before you pay to automate it.These shortcuts have limits. They do not prove the software can be built, they do not scale, and they can hide how much manual effort the real product will need. Be honest with users about how their data is handled. AI can play part of the wizard, for example by drafting replies, but a person should check the output before a customer relies on it.How do you set milestones and success metrics before building?Define milestones as working outcomes a person can try, not as lists of screens. "The login and dashboard pages are done" tells you little. "A new user can complete the booking journey on a phone and the clinic sees it" tells you the product works. Each milestone ends with a demo, so you can see progress, correct course early and stop if the evidence says so.A user can start and finish the core journey on a test account.The first real users can complete it without help from the team.The person on the other side, such as the admin or manager, can see and act on the result.Events are recorded so you can see where people drop out.A review compares what happened with the success metric you agreed.Set success metrics before you build, while you are still neutral. Choose one primary metric tied to the journey, such as the share of started journeys that finish or the number of users who return unprompted. Write down the threshold that counts as success and what you will do if you miss it. Without this, every result can be explained away.Instrumentation is how you get the data. At a minimum, record when a user starts the journey, each step they complete, where they leave and when they finish. Pair those numbers with short conversations, because analytics show what happened and people tell you why. Add tracking in the first milestone. A review of the journey with user experience design before you build often removes a whole round of rework. This is also how we work at Cubusify under Results as a Service: define the goal, deliver in milestones with demos and measure what changes.How can AI help plan an MVP without replacing user conversations?AI is useful for speed during planning and weak at the thing that matters most: telling you what real customers want. Use it to draft, summarise and prototype. Do not use it to decide. A language model can produce confident, plausible answers about customers who do not exist, and it will not warn you when it is wrong.Summarise and tag interview notes or transcripts, once participants have agreed and sensitive details are removed, then check the themes against the originals.Draft user stories, acceptance criteria and test cases that your team reviews and edits.Generate clickable prototypes and sample data so you can put something in front of users sooner.Scan public competitor material and documentation for questions worth asking, treating the output as leads to verify rather than facts.What AI cannot do is replace talking to ten real people. Synthetic personas and AI-generated "customer feedback" are not evidence. Treat AI as a way to prepare better conversations and to build the test faster, never as the test itself.When is an MVP the wrong tool?An MVP is the wrong tool when the question is already answered or when "minimum" is not acceptable. If you are automating a well-understood internal process, the requirements are known and you should build the full solution in milestones. If the product handles payments, health records or other regulated data, security and compliance cannot be trimmed to fit a first test. And if you cannot reach any real users, building will not fix that. Sometimes the cheaper test is no software at all: a landing page or a manual pilot. If one of those can answer your riskiest assumption, do that first.What to do nextThis week, write your one-sentence journey, list your assumptions and circle the riskiest. Then sort your feature list into must, should and could, and challenge every must. Bring that page, plus a sketch or your current spreadsheet, to a conversation. Concrete examples make scope easier to agree.If you would like a second pair of eyes, our MVP development work starts with exactly this: discovery, scope and a milestone plan. Cost and timeline depend on the scope, so the sensible first step is a short conversation. Talk to us about your MVP when you are ready.Discuss your projectFor clearer search foundations and useful answers, explore our SEO, AEO and GEO services.CONTINUE READINGAnother useful perspective.SEO, AEO and GEO: where should your business start? ↗Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom store? ↗Where AI automation is actually useful. ↗

      "title": "SEO, AEO and GEO: where should your business start? | Cubusify",
      "description": "A practical plan for clearer search visibility, useful answers and a website people can trust.",
      "h1": [
        "SEO, AEO and GEO: where should your business start?"
      ],
      "headings": [
        {
          "level": "H1",
          "text": "SEO, AEO and GEO: where should your business start?"
        },
        {
          "level": "H2",
          "text": "What to consider"
        },
        {
          "level": "H2",
          "text": "What do SEO, AEO and GEO mean?"
        },
        {
          "level": "H2",
          "text": "Choose one customer journey to improve"
        },
        {
          "level": "H2",
          "text": "Use structured data accurately"

          "level": "H2",
          "text": "Agree what success looks like"
        },

          "level": "H2",
          "text": "Another useful perspective."

      ],
      "words": 460,
      "text": "Home/Insights/SEARCH & GROWTHSEARCH & GROWTHSEO, AEO and GEO: where should your business start?A practical plan for clearer search visibility, useful answers and a website people can trust.By Cubusify Editorial · Updated 18 October 2026On this pageWhat do SEO, AEO and GEO mean?Choose one customer journey to improveUse structured data accuratelyAgree what success looks likeWhat to considerStart with your highest-priority service and the questions buyers ask before contacting you.Keep technical search foundations, content and conversion improvements in one plan.Measure qualified enquiries as well as visibility.A growing business usually has a practical question: what should we improve first to bring more suitable enquiries? Start with a service page that explains who you help, what you deliver and how a project begins. Search visibility is only useful when a visitor can understand the offer and take the next step.What do SEO, AEO and GEO mean?FocusWhat it meansUseful workSEOSearch engine optimizationCrawlable pages, clear structure and useful content.AEOAnswer engine optimizationClear responses to specific customer questions.GEOGenerative engine optimizationUseful, attributable information for AI-assisted discovery.Google’s current guidance treats optimization for its generative AI search features as part of SEO. The fundamentals still matter: useful original content, accessible pages and a clear technical structure. Eligibility does not guarantee indexing or inclusion. Read Google’s guide to generative AI search.Choose one customer journey to improveFor example, a manufacturer seeking a production dashboard needs to understand the problems it can solve, which systems it connects to, how implementation is scoped and what information to prepare. A page that answers those questions gives the buyer a more useful starting point than a long list of technologies.Choose a priority service and define the type of enquiry you want.List the questions your sales team hears repeatedly.Review the current page on a phone: can a buyer find the answer and contact you?Add relevant examples, a clear process and a practical next step.Check that page titles, links and navigation describe the actual content.Use structured data accuratelyStructured data describes page content in a machine-readable format. Use applicable types and keep the markup consistent with what visitors can see. It does not guarantee a rich result or AI citation. See Google’s structured data introduction.Agree what success looks likeRecord a baseline for the priority page before changing it.Track relevant search queries, landing-page visits and completed enquiries.Review enquiry quality: service fit, budget, location and readiness.Compare a meaningful period and account for seasonality before drawing conclusions.At Cubusify, we bring the technical review, page improvements and measurement plan together. Explore our SEO, AEO and GEO service, then share your website and the services you want to grow.Discuss your projectFor clearer search foundations and useful answers, explore our SEO, AEO and GEO services.CONTINUE READINGAnother useful perspective.Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom store? ↗Where AI automation is actually useful. ↗Plan a smaller, stronger first MVP. ↗",

      "text": "Home/Insights/ECOMMERCEECOMMERCEShopify, WooCommerce or a custom store?Start with your catalogue, operations and growth plans.By Cubusify Editorial · Updated 18 October 2026On this pageWhat is the real difference between Shopify, WooCommerce and a custom store?How large and complex is your catalogue?Who will run the store every day?What about integrations, ERP and checkout customisation?What does total cost of ownership include?How do performance, hosting and SEO control compare?Shopify vs WooCommerce vs custom: side-by-side comparisonWhen does headless or custom make sense, and what is the migration risk?What to do nextWhat to considerShopify is hosted and managed for you, WooCommerce is a WordPress plugin you host yourself, and a custom store is software built around your own rules.The deciding factors are usually who runs the store day to day, how complex your catalogue is, and which systems must connect to it, not the feature list.Compare total cost of ownership, not the build quote: hosting, apps or plugins, maintenance, payment fees and developer time all recur.Choose custom or headless only when a specific, revenue-relevant journey cannot be done on a standard platform.Replatforming carries real SEO and data risk, so plan URL redirects, product data migration and a rollback path before you commit.Shopify vs WooCommerce comes down to who runs the store and how unusual your way of selling is. Shopify is a hosted platform that looks after the infrastructure for you. WooCommerce is a plugin for WordPress that you host and maintain yourself. A custom store is worth building only when a standard platform cannot support a journey that earns you money.The best choice is rarely the platform with the longest feature list. It is the one your team can run on an ordinary Tuesday without calling a developer, and that will still fit the business in two years. This guide gives you the criteria, a comparison table and a short process for deciding.What is the real difference between Shopify, WooCommerce and a custom store?The real difference is who carries responsibility. With Shopify, a vendor hosts the platform, runs the checkout infrastructure and ships core updates, and you configure the store, choose a theme and add apps. With WooCommerce, you or your agency choose hosting, update WordPress, the plugin and every extension, and take care of security and backups. With a custom store, you own all of it.That gives you a simple way to think about it. Shopify trades some flexibility for convenience. WooCommerce trades convenience for control over the code, the database and the content. Custom trades speed and low upkeep for the freedom to model your business exactly. None of the three is better in general. Each is better for a particular kind of team.How large and complex is your catalogue?Catalogue complexity matters more than catalogue size. A few thousand simple products with sizes and colours suit all three options. Trouble starts with unusual structures: made-to-order products with many dependent options, bundles with rules, B2B price lists per customer, rental or booking items, or products that need a configurator before they can be priced.Ask three questions. Can every product be described as a title, images, variants and a price? Do prices or availability depend on who is buying? Does a buyer need to configure the product before adding it to the basket? If the answers are yes, no and no, a hosted platform is usually the quickest route. If the second or third answer is yes, list exactly which rules you need and check whether a maintained app or plugin covers them before you consider custom work.Who will run the store every day?The person who edits products, processes orders and runs promotions should shape the decision. A marketing or operations lead who wants to launch a collection or a discount without developer help usually does well on Shopify, because the admin is built for merchants. A team that already publishes content on WordPress may find WooCommerce natural, because products, posts and landing pages live in one system.Custom admin tools can be excellent when they are designed around your exact workflow, but they only help if someone owns their evolution. Be honest about capacity. If nobody on the team can look after plugin updates, backups and hosting, a self-hosted store will slowly become a risk. If you want deep control and have a developer or agency on retainer, that same setup becomes an asset.Rule of thumbChoose the platform your least technical daily user can operate confidently. A powerful system that only one developer understands is a business risk, not an advantage.What about integrations, ERP and checkout customisation?Integrations decide more projects than design does. Write down every system the store must exchange data with: inventory or ERP, accounting, shipping, a CRM, a marketing tool, a returns process. For each one, note what moves in which direction and how often. Stock levels and orders are the usual pain points, because errors there cost money and customer trust.Shopify extends through apps and APIs, and its documentation describes checkout customisation through checkout UI extensions and Shopify Functions, which let you add interface elements and change business logic such as discounts, delivery options and payment rules. WooCommerce is extended with PHP hooks, filters, plugins and its REST API, so almost anything is possible but quality varies by plugin. A custom store lets you design the integration properly, at the price of building and maintaining it.If you run an ERP, ask early whether a maintained connector exists for your platform and who supports it when it breaks. Our integration solutions work often starts exactly here, with a clear data map between the store and the systems behind it.Related interface showcase. Illustrates product capabilities; it is not evidence of a client result.What does total cost of ownership include?Total cost of ownership is everything you pay to build, run and change the store over its life, not the build quote. Prices and plans change often, so check each vendor’s current pricing page rather than relying on an article. What you should do is list the cost categories so the three options are compared like for like.Platform or hosting: a subscription for a hosted platform, or hosting, a CDN and backups for a self-hosted one.Theme and design work, including future changes to templates.Apps or plugins, which often carry their own recurring fees, and the effort of keeping them compatible.Payment provider and transaction fees, which depend on your provider, region and plan.Developer time for integrations, bug fixes, updates and security patching.Staff time: how many hours a week your team spends working around limitations.Migration and exit costs if you outgrow the choice.Custom builds have the highest upfront cost and often the lowest per-feature friction later, but they also have the largest maintenance obligation. Hosted platforms look cheaper at the start and can accumulate app fees. Self-hosted WooCommerce can look cheapest on paper and then quietly cost developer hours. Model three years, not three months.How do performance, hosting and SEO control compare?Hosting responsibility is the clearest performance difference. On Shopify the platform handles servers and delivery, so your speed depends mostly on your theme, images and apps. On WooCommerce, speed also depends on your host, caching, database and plugin load, which gives you more control and more ways to go wrong. On a custom store, performance is whatever you engineer.For search, all three can rank well when built properly. WooCommerce sits on WordPress and offers fine control over URLs, templates and content. Shopify gives you editable titles, descriptions, redirects and sitemaps, though some URL patterns such as the products and collections prefixes are fixed. Custom stores give full control but require you to build SEO basics deliberately. Whichever route you take, plan for performance and search foundations, clean product data and structured markup from the start.Shopify vs WooCommerce vs custom: side-by-side comparisonUse this table to score each option against your own priorities. It describes general tendencies, not guarantees, so confirm the details for your own requirements before you decide. Give each row a weight from one to three based on how much it matters to your business, then see which column wins.Shopify, WooCommerce and custom ecommerce compared across the main decision criteriaCriterionShopifyWooCommerceCustom storeHosting modelHosted and managed by the vendorSelf-hosted on WordPress; you choose and manage hostingYou choose and manage everythingBest for catalogueStandard products and variantsContent-rich or moderately unusual cataloguesComplex configurators, rules and pricingDay-to-day adminMerchant-friendly, built for non-developersFamiliar if you already use WordPress; more upkeepWhatever is built; needs an ownerCheckout customisationThrough extensions and Shopify FunctionsHooks, filters and plugins; wide but uneven qualityFully designed to your rulesIntegrations and ERPApps and APIs; check connector supportPlugins and REST API; check maintenanceBuilt to your exact data flowsCost shape over timeSubscription plus apps and feesHosting, plugins and developer timeHighest upfront, ongoing engineeringPerformance responsibilityPlatform infrastructure; you manage theme and appsShared: host, caching, pluginsEntirely yoursSEO controlGood, with some fixed URL patternsVery high with WordPress toolingTotal, but built from scratchMigration risk laterModerate; data export and redirects neededModerate; you own the data and databaseHigher; custom data models are harder to moveWhen does headless or custom make sense, and what is the migration risk?Custom or headless commerce makes sense when a specific journey earns real revenue and a standard platform cannot support it. Headless means the shopping interface is built separately from the commerce engine and talks to it through an API. It can give you a faster, fully tailored front end, but it also means you maintain two layers, and many conveniences of a themed store become your responsibility.Good reasons include a product configurator, unusual B2B pricing, a subscription model with special rules, or an experience that spans content, community and commerce. Weak reasons include wanting a unique look alone, or assuming custom is automatically faster. Our custom ecommerce team tends to suggest proving the hardest journey with a small prototype first.Replatforming itself is risky whichever way you go. Products, customers, order history, reviews and URLs all have to move, and any URL that changes without a redirect can lose search visibility. Keep the old store running until the new one is verified, redirect every important URL, and agree a rollback path. Our search and visibility service includes a review of redirects, indexing and monitoring needs.Related interface showcase. Illustrates product capabilities; it is not evidence of a client result.What to do nextTake an hour and do three things. List your ten most important products and any rules attached to them. List every system the store must connect to. Name the person who will run the store daily. With those three lists, most teams can already rule out one option.Then test the hardest journey, not the easiest. If you are leaning towards a hosted platform, our Shopify development work focuses on theme, catalogue and checkout. If WordPress is already part of your stack, see WooCommerce development. If neither fits, bring your list to a conversation and we will help you judge it honestly. You can contact us whenever you are ready.Discuss your projectFor clearer search foundations and useful answers, explore our SEO, AEO and GEO services.CONTINUE READINGAnother useful perspective.SEO, AEO and GEO: where should your business start? ↗Where AI automation is actually useful. ↗Plan a smaller, stronger first MVP. ↗",

      "text": "Home/Insights/AI & AUTOMATIONAI & AUTOMATIONWhere AI automation is actually useful.Look for repeatable work before choosing a model.By Cubusify Editorial · Updated 18 October 2026On this pageWhat makes a task worth automating with AI?Which seven workflows should you automate first?How do you rank the seven for your business?What should you not automate yet?How do you run a first pilot?What to do nextWhat to considerAI automation for business works best on tasks that repeat often, have a clear owner and can be checked quickly by a person.Start with workflows where a mistake is cheap to catch, such as drafting replies for approval, before touching anything that moves money or sends messages on its own.Every workflow needs a number you can measure before and after, such as minutes per task, first response time or share of drafts accepted without edits.Rank candidates by frequency, cost of error, data availability and ease, then pilot one workflow on real examples before building more.Some work should not be automated yet: unclear processes, high-stakes decisions and anything with no sample data to test against.AI automation for business means using AI models inside a defined workflow so that software handles the routine reading, sorting and drafting, while people handle the decisions. It is most useful on tasks that repeat often, follow a recognisable pattern and can be checked quickly.It is least useful when sold as a replacement for judgement. This guide gives seven workflows that usually make good first projects, a table to rank them for your own business, and a list of work that should wait. Each workflow is described the same way: what goes in, what the AI does, what a person still checks, and how to measure it.What makes a task worth automating with AI?A task is worth automating when it repeats often, has a clear owner, produces an output someone can check in seconds, and has examples you can test against. If you cannot describe the input, the expected output and what counts as a mistake, the task is not ready for AI yet.Four questions help. How often does it happen? What does a wrong result cost? Do you have past examples to test with? How many other systems must it connect to? A weekly task with expensive errors and no examples is a poor first project. A daily task with cheap errors and a shared inbox full of examples is a good one. Write down the current time per task before you start, because that is your baseline for every claim later.Which seven workflows should you automate first?These seven appear in most small and mid-sized businesses in some form. They are listed roughly from lowest risk to highest. In every case the AI prepares and a person approves, at least until you have evidence that the output is reliable enough to relax that rule.1. Enquiry triage and routingGoes in: emails, web form messages or chat enquiries.AI does: labels the type (sales, support, billing, spam), extracts key details such as company, product and urgency, and routes it to the right queue.Person checks: low-confidence items and a regular sample of routed ones.Measure: time from arrival to the right person seeing it, and the share of enquiries rerouted by hand.This is often the best first project because mistakes are visible and cheap to fix. A misrouted enquiry is slower, not catastrophic. Our business automation service typically starts here.2. Drafting replies for human approvalGoes in: a customer message plus your policies, past replies and product information.AI does: writes a draft reply in your tone and cites which policy or past answer it used.Person checks: every draft before it is sent, editing as needed.Measure: drafts accepted with no or light edits, minutes saved per reply, and complaints about tone or accuracy.Nothing is sent without approval, so the risk stays low while you learn how often the drafts are good. Edits are also useful data: patterns in what people change show you where the instructions or source documents need work.3. Document and invoice data extractionGoes in: invoices, purchase orders, forms, contracts or delivery notes, often as PDFs or photos.AI does: pulls out named fields such as supplier, date, line items and totals into a structured record.Person checks: fields that fail validation, such as totals that do not add up, and a sample of the rest.Measure: field-level accuracy against a hand-checked set, and time per document.Accuracy here can be measured field by field, which makes it one of the more honest workflows to evaluate. Add simple rules around the AI, for example rejecting a record where line items do not sum to the total.4. Meeting and call note summaries into the CRMGoes in: a call recording transcript or meeting notes, with permission from participants.AI does: summarises decisions, lists action items with owners, and proposes updates to CRM fields.Person checks: the summary and any CRM change before it is saved.Measure: minutes spent on admin after calls, and how many CRM records are complete a day later.The value is mostly consistency: notes get written and records get updated. Make sure you have consent to record and transcribe, and decide where transcripts are stored and for how long. A custom CRM can make the proposed updates easier to review.5. Internal knowledge searchGoes in: handbooks, policies, product sheets, past proposals and help articles.AI does: answers staff questions in plain language and shows the source passages it used.Person checks: the cited source when the answer matters, and owners review gaps the assistant reports.Measure: questions answered without asking a colleague, share of answers with a correct source, and searches that end in no result.This is the workflow behind most AI assistants. It only works as well as your documents, so budget time to clean them. Explore how a business AI assistant can use your own information with appropriate access controls.Related interface showcase. Illustrates product capabilities; it is not evidence of a client result.6. Lead qualification and follow-up prepGoes in: new leads from forms, ads or events, plus your definition of a good fit.AI does: summarises the company from public information, scores fit against your criteria, and drafts a first follow-up for the salesperson.Person checks: the score and the draft before anyone is contacted.Measure: time from lead to first contact, and whether high-scored leads convert better than low-scored ones.Track the last measure honestly. If scores do not predict outcomes, change the criteria rather than trust the number. See our sales and marketing automation work for how routing and follow-up preparation fit together.7. Report and dashboard commentaryGoes in: figures from your reports or business dashboards, plus last period for comparison.AI does: drafts a short written commentary on what changed and which numbers look unusual.Person checks: every figure quoted and every explanation offered, since the AI sees the numbers but not the reasons.Measure: time to produce the weekly report, and corrections made before it is shared.Keep the calculations in code or your reporting tool, not in the model. Let the AI describe numbers that are already computed, then have an analyst confirm the explanations.How do you rank the seven for your business?Score each candidate on four things: how often it happens, how costly a mistake is, whether you have example data, and how easy it is to connect. The table below shows a typical starting view. Treat the ratings as a prompt for discussion, because your business will differ.Typical starting ratings. Adjust to your own volumes and risks.WorkflowFrequencyCost of errorData availabilityEaseEnquiry triage and routingHighLowHigh (inbox history)MediumDraft replies for approvalHighLow (approved first)High (sent mail)MediumDocument and invoice extractionMedium to highMediumMediumMediumMeeting and call notes to CRMMediumLow to mediumMediumMediumInternal knowledge searchMediumLow to mediumDepends on document qualityMediumLead qualification and follow-up prepMediumMediumMediumMedium to hardReport and dashboard commentaryLow to medium (weekly)MediumHigh (the numbers exist)Easy to mediumPick the row where frequency is high, error cost is low and data exists. For many teams that is enquiry triage or drafted replies. If your biggest pain is somewhere else, such as invoices, start there, but add stricter validation because the cost of an error is higher.Rule of thumbIf you would be uncomfortable with a new hire doing the task on day one without review, the AI should not do it without review either. Begin with review, then relax it where your measurements justify it.What should you not automate yet?Leave a task alone when the process is unclear, a wrong answer is costly or irreversible, or you have no examples to test against. Automating a messy process produces a faster mess. These tasks are better left with people, or automated only up to a drafting step.Processes nobody can describe. Write the steps down first. If two people do it differently, agree one way before adding AI.Final decisions on money, contracts, hiring, health or legal matters. AI can prepare material, but a named person decides.Anything that sends messages or changes records with no review, until you have measured error rates on real examples.Tasks with no sample data. Without 30 to 50 real, representative cases you cannot tell whether the workflow works.Sensitive personal or confidential data you have not classified. Decide what may leave your systems before choosing tools.Rare, high-variety work such as one-off negotiations, where each case is different and the saving is small.How do you run a first pilot?Run one workflow, on real examples, with a person approving the output, and compare it with your baseline. A small pilot answers whether the workflow works for your data far more cheaply than a large build, and it shows where the real work is: usually in documents, permissions and integrations, not the model.Choose one workflow and write down its current time per task and error rate.Collect 30 to 50 real examples, including awkward ones, and agree what a good output looks like.Build the smallest version that connects to the real inbox, CRM or document store, with approval before anything is sent or saved.Run it alongside the current process for a set period and log accepted, edited and rejected outputs.Review the numbers, fix the biggest failure pattern, then decide whether to widen, change or stop.Related interface showcase. Illustrates product capabilities; it is not evidence of a client result.Plan for the unglamorous parts too: logging, access rights, a clear handoff when the AI is unsure, and someone who owns the workflow after launch. Demos show the idea; production needs these. If you are unsure whether you need a simple assistant, a workflow or something more autonomous, explore our AI and automation services first.What to do nextPick the workflow with the highest frequency, lowest cost of error and best example data, and measure how long it takes today. That one number is the start of a useful conversation about scope. You do not need a model chosen or a vendor shortlisted to do this.If you would like help ranking your own candidates or scoping a pilot, tell us which task is eating the most time through our contact page. We work in milestones with regular demos and agree what success looks like before building. Cost and timing depend on scope, so we talk them through with you rather than quote a number here.Discuss your projectFor clearer search foundations and useful answers, explore our SEO, AEO and GEO services.CONTINUE READINGAnother useful perspective.SEO, AEO and GEO: where should your business start? ↗Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom store? ↗Plan a smaller, stronger first MVP. ↗",
